extracted.intended_audience: food scientists, refrigeration engineers, and others concerned with industrial food preservation (e.g., policymakers, technologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for freezing, storing, and thawing foodstuffs to preserve their physical, chemical, and nutritive qualities; compares methods (air vs brine), rates of cooling, and storage/thawing practices with attention to food type (fish, meat, plant tissues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer freezing (well below freezing point) over chilling when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the two refrigerative processes—chilling and freezing—the former is much inferior. In this process the temperature is kept at about 0°C ... In the freezing process, on the other hand, the temperature of storage is kept well below the freezing point of the food substance, which consequently becomes frozen into a solid block...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freezing greatly reduces chemical reaction velocities (roughly halving reaction rates per 10°C fall) and inhibits micro-organism growth; therefore, where practicable aim to transfer foods from chilling (≈0°C) to true freezing (well below freezing point) to better arrest putrefactive processes and prolong storage life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate of cooling — rapid freezing to minimise irreversible changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid cooling produces a fine-grained frozen mass, and, if this is sufficiently finely grained, the original structure of the sol or gel is restored on thawing. Conversely, slow freezing can produce visible 'flocks' (e.g., chlorophyll hydrosols) and irreversible changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design freezing processes to achieve rapid cooling whenever target food structures (sols, gels, cells, tissues) are likely to regain their original condition on thawing. Use brine-immersion or other rapid methods where structural reversibility and minimal histological damage are priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of freezing method (air freezing vs brine/salt-solution freezing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practically there are only two general methods employed in the freezing of foods on the large scale: freezing in cold air, and in a cold brine solution respectively. Each method has obvious advantages and disadvantages...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select method based on the trade-off between speed (brine = faster) and risks (brine = salt penetration, possible chemical reactions affecting appearance/taste; air = slower, more desiccation). Match method to the specific food (e.g., brine may benefit fish by reducing histological change; air may be preferable for some meats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise desiccation for susceptible foods (e.g., fish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fish depreciates rapidly by desiccation, but is not very liable to attack by micro-organisms; meat, on the other hand, does not lose water readily, but favours the growth of moulds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preserving foods prone to desiccation (notably fish), prioritise freezing and storage methods that reduce water loss (e.g., faster freezing, protective coverings, choice of medium) even if that means accepting other trade-offs; conversely, for foods that favour microbial growth, emphasise controls that limit micro-organisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and minimise salt penetration when using brine freezing
rubrics_metrics.description: Brine freezing gives much more rapid cooling, but food cell contents may pass outwards into the cooling medium, and salt may also pass from the latter into the tissues of the food. Penetration of salt into the food material is in some cases (i.e. fish) not objectionable, but in certain instances chemical action may occur between the foodstuff and the salt with undesirable consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If brine/salt solutions are used, select physical conditions (temperature, immersion time, salt type/concentration) to minimise undesirable penetration; consider alternative salts or mitigation strategies where salt–food chemical reactions (e.g., pigment alteration) reduce market value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chemical reactions between freezing medium and food (appearance/taste impacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reaction takes place between the salt and the pigment of the beef which so changes the appearance of the latter that its market value may be considerably reduced... conversion of hemoglobin into methemoglobin causes discoloration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess chemical compatibility of chosen freezing medium with food components (pigments, lipids). Where reactions cause discoloration or off-flavors (e.g., beef in brine), either avoid that medium or develop means to prevent the reaction (alter salt, add barriers, modify process parameters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage temperature and conditions must be tailored to each food
rubrics_metrics.description: All these changes (evaporation, chemical changes, growth of moulds and bacteria) can be retarded by lowering the temperature of the storage chambers, but economic conditions impose a limit... the conditions in storage chambers should, it may be emphasised, be different for different foods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose storage temperatures and chamber environments specific to the food type to minimise evaporation of volatiles, autolysis, fat hydrolysis/oxidation, and microbial growth, while accounting for economic limits on temperature; avoid a one-size-fits-all storage temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thawing rate affects final product character — manage thawing carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief summary of the available information concerning thawing of food. This side of the subject is not without importance, since the rate of thawing of frozen food has a significant effect upon its character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control thawing rates appropriate to the food and to desired texture/juice retention. Evaluate thawing protocols as part of overall preservation design because poor thawing can negate gains from optimal freezing and storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to restore the original condition — success metric for preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: This method of preservation involves freezing, storage in the frozen state, and finally thawing of the frozen material, and the more nearly the condition of the food-stuff so treated resembles the original, the more successful has the storage been from the economic as well as the physiological standpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use resemblance to the fresh state (appearance, texture, flavour, nutritive value, drip loss) as the primary measure of preservation success; design freezing/storage/thawing to maximise resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and limit physical and chemical degradations during storage
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical changes, such as evaporation of water and aromatic flavouring substances, chemical changes including autolytic reactions, hydrolysis of fats and oxidation of the hydrolytic products, and finally the growth of moulds and bacteria, must be guarded against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Storage systems should address (a) vapour barriers and humidity control to prevent evaporative loss, (b) antioxidant or temperature regimes to limit fat hydrolysis and oxidation, (c) enzymatic/autolytic activity mitigation, and (d) microbiological controls appropriate to the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess retention of vitamins and nutritive factors under freezing
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential importance of the vitamins for animal nutrition has made it necessary to ascertain the influence of low temperatures upon these accessory food substances... it has been shown that the vitamin content of butter is undiminished by preservation in this way; investigations of the effect of low temperatures upon the antiscorbutic vitamins are at present in progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include assays of vitamin content and other nutritive factors when validating freezing/storage methods; do not assume universal stability — test each nutrient/food combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for enzyme survival and activity post-freezing
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally speaking, enzymes survive exposure to the temperatures employed in refrigeration, and can exercise their catalytic functions when temperature and environment again become normal; in some cases, indeed, the catalytic activity may be increased by exposure to low temperatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider residual enzymatic activity as a driver of post-thaw changes (flavour, texture, spoilage) and design pre-treatment (e.g., blanching), temperature profiles, or inhibitors accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate brine-immersion freezing for meat carefully (drip loss vs discoloration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small preliminary experiments indicated that rapid freezing by immersion in cold brine was an effective way of preservation so far as absence of drip, and appearance and flavour of the product after thawing were concerned. ... One rather serious objection ... discoloration of the surface layers of the lean of the meat owing to the conversion of hemoglobin into methemoglobin. The discoloration detracts seriously from the appearance and market value of the meat...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering brine immersion for meat, weigh the benefit of reduced drip and improved post-thaw appearance/flavour against the risk of pigment alteration and market-value loss; further experimental work and process refinement (to prevent methemoglobin formation) are required before widespread adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select freezing and storage technology consistent with economic constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: All these changes can be retarded by lowering the temperature of the storage chambers, but economic conditions impose a limit at which reduction of temperature must stop. It becomes... a question of selecting the least injurious conditions for each particular food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimization should balance quality preservation and operational cost; set target temperatures and process parameters that give acceptable quality within realistic economic bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and design for minimum drip (weight loss) on thawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Beef which has been preserved in the frozen state is frequently inferior to fresh beef on account of the drip of meat juice which occurs on thawing. This loss may amount to as much as 15 per cent. of the weight of the meat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include drip-loss measurements as a key performance metric for meat freezing processes; aim to minimise drip (through rapid freezing, process selection, or pre/post treatments) to preserve weight and quality.
